newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mubarak suggests incentives for desert project.
newsitem.headline: Mubarak suggests incentives for desert project.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak told his government on Sunday that a giant project to irrigate the Western Desert was an absolute necessity and it should look at special incentives for foreign investment in the scheme.

In a speech opening a new session of parliament, Mubarak said that within 20 years the number of Egyptians would grow to 85 million from 60 million now and the Nile Valley and Delta could not possibly accommodate the extra 25 million people.
The vast majority of Egyptians have lived for millennia on the land irrigated by the Nile but this amounts to only about four percent of Egypt. The rest is desert.
The answer, Mubarak said, was a complete review of population distribution and a serious invasion of desert areas.

Mubarak's plan, inspired by the Nile reaching the highest level ever behind the High Dam at Aswan, is to divert water into the Western Desert and irrigate 500,000 acres (200,000 hectares) of land there.
After the level of the lake reached 178 metres above sea level last month, water spilt out of the lake westwards into the Toshka overflow canal for the first time ever.
The next stage will be to dig a canal northwards from the Toshka depression to irrigate what the government says is fertile land ready for reclamation.
"For us to see this giant national project implemented, I call on the government to start immediately...to start digging the north Toshka canal," Mubarak said.

"I call on investors, Egyptians and non-Egyptians, to come to this area with their investments, their projects and their ideas. I give the government the task of studying new advantages to investors in the valley to be set up, on top of the advantages set out in the laws now in force," he added.
"The concept of invading the desert is no longer a mere slogan or a dream to which we aspire. It has become a necessity imposed by population growth," he said.

Foreign economists have said they are dubious about the scheme, especially as the level of the High Dam lake will soon go down and the water would then have to be pumped up into the Toshka canal at great expense.
It would make more sense to use the extra water to irrigate new areas on the edges of the Nile Valley, where the climate is milder and manpower is readily available, they say.
The government newspaper al-Akhbar said on Sunday that a consultative committee had agreed work should start on digging a canal 30 km (20 miles) long north from the Toshka depression.
The minister of public works and water resources, Abdel-Hadi Radi, has said the first stage of the project will cost $1 billion and three billion pounds -- a total of $1.9 billion.

Mubarak described Egypt as one of the most attractive destinations in the world for foreign investment but said nothing about the Middle East and North Africa economic conference opening in Cairo on Tuesday.
